items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a set of reasons and evidence given to persuade the reader to accept a conclusion”?
items.answer: Argument
items.markingKey: Argument: a set of reasons and evidence given to persuade the reader to accept a conclusion. [1]

items.stem: Read the argument about the spread of online disinformation during elections. “The 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal showed that data from millions of Facebook users had been harvested for political targeting. False political content can change how people vote. Moreover, platforms profit from the engagement that false content attracts. So platforms have both the power and the incentive to shape elections. Some people claim that this would turn private companies into censors of political speech. However, the law could be limited to clearly false factual claims, such as the wrong polling date. Therefore, social media companies should be legally responsible for false political content.” What is the function of “However, the law could be limited to clearly false factual claims, such as the wrong polling date.” in this argument?
items.answer: Response to a counter-assertion
items.markingKey: “However, the law could be limited to clearly false factual claims, such as the wrong polling date.” is the response to a counter-assertion. [1]

items.stem: Mateo wrote this argument for a school debate: “A 2019 study by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology found higher false-match rates for some demographic groups in many algorithms. It records everyone, not only suspects. Moreover, mistaken identifications fall more often on some ethnic groups. So the technology threatens the rights of innocent people. Some people claim that the technology helps police find missing people and dangerous suspects. However, these aims can be met with targeted searches authorised by a judge. Therefore, governments should ban live facial recognition in public places.” What is the function of “It records everyone, not only suspects.” in this argument?
items.answer: Reason
items.markingKey: “It records everyone, not only suspects.” is the reason. [1]

items.stem: This argument appeared in an opinion column in Bangkok: “(1) The UN Human Rights Committee ruled in the Teitiota case (2020) that states may not return people to places where climate change threatens their right to life. (2) They are forced to leave their homes through no fault of their own. (3) Moreover, the countries that caused most emissions have a duty to help those harmed. (4) So climate migrants deserve the same protection as other forcibly displaced people. (5) Some people claim that widening the definition could weaken protection for people fleeing persecution. (6) However, a separate protocol could protect climate migrants without changing the 1951 Convention. (7) Therefore, people displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status.” Explain how the evidence supports the argument.
items.answer: It gives a real example/data (the UN Human Rights Committee ruled in the Teitiota case (2020) that states may not return people to places where climate change threatens their right to life) that makes the reason more credible and links to the conclusion that people displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies what evidence shows; 1 mark links it to reason/conclusion [2]

items.stem: This argument appeared in an opinion column in Muscat: “(1) People displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status. (2) They are forced to leave their homes through no fault of their own. (3) For example: The UN Human Rights Committee ruled in the Teitiota case (2020) that states may not return people to places where climate change threatens their right to life. (4) Furthermore, the countries that caused most emissions have a duty to help those harmed. (5) This shows that climate migrants deserve the same protection as other forcibly displaced people. (6) It is sometimes argued that widening the definition could weaken protection for people fleeing persecution. (7) But a separate protocol could protect climate migrants without changing the 1951 Convention.” (a) Identify the intermediate conclusion. (b) Identify two reasons given to support the intermediate conclusion.
items.answer: (a) Climate migrants deserve the same protection as other forcibly displaced people (sentence 5). (b) They are forced to leave their homes through no fault of their own; the countries that caused most emissions have a duty to help those harmed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Read the argument about migration caused by climate change. “(1) The UN Human Rights Committee ruled in the Teitiota case (2020) that states may not return people to places where climate change threatens their right to life. (2) They are forced to leave their homes through no fault of their own. (3) Moreover, the countries that caused most emissions have a duty to help those harmed. (4) So climate migrants deserve the same protection as other forcibly displaced people. (5) Some people claim that widening the definition could weaken protection for people fleeing persecution. (6) However, a separate protocol could protect climate migrants without changing the 1951 Convention. (7) Therefore, people displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status.” (a) Identify the intermediate conclusion. (b) Identify the evidence used. (c) Identify the counter-assertion and explain how the author responds to it.
items.answer: (a) Climate migrants deserve the same protection as other forcibly displaced people (sentence 4). (b) The UN Human Rights Committee ruled in the Teitiota case (2020) that states may not return people to places where climate change threatens their right to life (sentence 1). (c) Counter-assertion: widening the definition could weaken protection for people fleeing persecution. Response: a separate protocol could protect climate migrants without changing the 1951 Convention.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark [1] (c) 1 mark counter; 1 mark response [2]

items.stem: Read the argument about state use of facial recognition surveillance. “(1) Governments should ban live facial recognition in public places. (2) It records everyone, not only suspects. (3) For example: A 2019 study by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology found higher false-match rates for some demographic groups in many algorithms. (4) Furthermore, mistaken identifications fall more often on some ethnic groups. (5) This shows that the technology threatens the rights of innocent people. (6) It is sometimes argued that the technology helps police find missing people and dangerous suspects. (7) But these aims can be met with targeted searches authorised by a judge.” (a) Identify the main conclusion and the intermediate conclusion. (b) Suggest a further piece of evidence that would strengthen the argument.
items.answer: (a) MC: governments should ban live facial recognition in public places. IC: the technology threatens the rights of innocent people. (b) Comparative data from several countries, or a peer-reviewed study showing the effect claimed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark relevant evidence; 1 mark why it strengthens [2]

items.stem: Read the argument about reform of the UN Security Council. “(1) The veto power of the permanent members should be restricted. (2) A single country can block action supported by most of the world. (3) For example: Russia has vetoed draft resolutions on the war in Syria many times since 2011. (4) Furthermore, the permanent members were chosen in 1945 and do not reflect today’s world. (5) This shows that the veto prevents the Council from fulfilling its responsibility for international peace. (6) It is sometimes argued that the veto keeps the great powers inside the UN system. (7) But a restriction only in cases of mass atrocities would leave most of their influence intact.” (a) Describe the structure of the argument. (b) Suggest a further piece of evidence that would strengthen the argument.
items.answer: (a) Two reasons (with evidence) support the intermediate conclusion, which supports the main conclusion; a counter-assertion is raised and answered. (b) Comparative data from several countries, or a peer-reviewed study showing the effect claimed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reasons → IC; 1 mark IC → MC; 1 mark counter/response [3] (b) 1 mark relevant evidence; 1 mark why it strengthens [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a statement that something is the case, which may or may not be supported”?
items.answer: Claim
items.markingKey: Claim: a statement that something is the case, which may or may not be supported. [1]

items.stem: Read the argument about reform of the UN Security Council. “Russia has vetoed draft resolutions on the war in Syria many times since 2011. A single country can block action supported by most of the world. Moreover, the permanent members were chosen in 1945 and do not reflect today’s world. So the veto prevents the Council from fulfilling its responsibility for international peace. Some people claim that the veto keeps the great powers inside the UN system. However, a restriction only in cases of mass atrocities would leave most of their influence intact. Therefore, the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted.” What is the function of “So the veto prevents the Council from fulfilling its responsibility for international peace.” in this argument?
items.answer: Intermediate conclusion
items.markingKey: “So the veto prevents the Council from fulfilling its responsibility for international peace.” is the intermediate conclusion. [1]

items.stem: In an argument that economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour, the author writes: “Targeted governments can blame foreigners for economic hardship” and “Decades of US sanctions on Cuba since the 1960s have not changed its system of government”. Explain the difference between the role of these two statements.
items.answer: The first is a reason: a general claim that supports the conclusion. The second is evidence: a specific fact or example used to support a reason and make it more convincing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason identified and explained; 1 mark evidence identified and explained [2]

items.stem: Read the argument about disputes over shared rivers. “(1) The Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan (1960) has survived several wars. (2) Downstream countries depend on the river for drinking water and farming. (3) Moreover, agreed rules reduce the risk of conflict. (4) So shared rules can make water a source of cooperation rather than conflict. (5) Some people claim that upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory. (6) However, international water law also requires them not to cause significant harm to others. (7) Therefore, upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours.” Identify the intermediate conclusion.
items.answer: Shared rules can make water a source of cooperation rather than conflict (sentence 4).
items.markingKey: 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Zara argues that governments should repeal broad “false news” laws. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence. You may wish to consider: assumptions; counter-arguments.
items.answer: For: Such laws are vague and let officials decide what is true. Press freedom organisations have documented journalists jailed under “false news” laws in several countries. A free press is needed to expose corruption. Against: False reports can cause panic during a crisis. The argument assumes that governments cannot be trusted to judge fairly what counts as false news. Judgement: Judgement weighs the reasons and evidence against the counter-argument (response offered: existing laws on defamation and incitement already deal with genuinely harmful falsehoods).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

(b) Suggest a further piece of evidence that would strengthen the argument.
items.answer: (a) MC: governments should ban live facial recognition in public places. IC: the technology threatens the rights of innocent people. (b) Comparative data from several countries, or a peer-reviewed study showing the effect claimed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark relevant evidence; 1 mark why it strengthens [2]

items.stem: Assess the claim that voting should be made compulsory.
items.answer: For: A democracy works best when governments are chosen by the whole electorate. In Australia, where voting is compulsory, turnout is usually above 90%. Compulsory voting forces parties to address the needs of groups that currently stay at home. Against: Compulsory voting removes the freedom not to vote. The argument assumes that governments chosen by more of the electorate will be more representative of the electorate’s interests. Judgement: Judgement weighs the reasons and evidence against the counter-argument (response offered: voters may still spoil their ballot or choose “none of the above”).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “an unstated reason that the argument depends on: if it is false, the conclusion does not follow”?
items.answer: Assumption
items.markingKey: Assumption: an unstated reason that the argument depends on: if it is false, the conclusion does not follow. [1]

items.stem: Aisha wrote this argument for a school debate: “The UN Human Rights Committee ruled in the Teitiota case (2020) that states may not return people to places where climate change threatens their right to life. They are forced to leave their homes through no fault of their own. Moreover, the countries that caused most emissions have a duty to help those harmed. So climate migrants deserve the same protection as other forcibly displaced people. Some people claim that widening the definition could weaken protection for people fleeing persecution. However, a separate protocol could protect climate migrants without changing the 1951 Convention. Therefore, people displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status.” Which of the following is an assumption the argument relies on?
options: Being forced to leave home is the key feature that should define who is a refugee
Climate migrants deserve the same protection as other forcibly displaced people
Exporting countries could manage the waste better at home
They are forced to leave their homes through no fault of their own
items.answer: Being forced to leave home is the key feature that should define who is a refugee
items.markingKey: Assumption: being forced to leave home is the key feature that should define who is a refugee. The reason and IC are stated, so they are not assumptions; the fourth option is irrelevant. [1]

items.stem: This argument appeared in an opinion column in Auckland: “Voting should be made compulsory. A democracy works best when governments are chosen by the whole electorate. For example: In Australia, where voting is compulsory, turnout is usually above 90%. Furthermore, compulsory voting forces parties to address the needs of groups that currently stay at home. This shows that compulsory voting would make elected governments more representative. It is sometimes argued that compulsory voting removes the freedom not to vote. But voters may still spoil their ballot or choose “none of the above”.” Which of the following is an assumption the argument relies on?
options: Governments chosen by more of the electorate will be more representative of the electorate’s interests
The purpose of sanctions is to change the target’s behaviour rather than to signal disapproval
A democracy works best when governments are chosen by the whole electorate
Compulsory voting would make elected governments more representative
items.answer: Governments chosen by more of the electorate will be more representative of the electorate’s interests
items.markingKey: Assumption: governments chosen by more of the electorate will be more representative of the electorate’s interests. The reason and IC are stated, so they are not assumptions; the fourth option is irrelevant. [1]

items.stem: Read this argument: “The new anti-corruption agency in Lunaria has charged 40 officials this year. It follows that corruption in Lunaria is falling.” Identify the assumption, explain why it may be false, and explain the effect on the argument.
items.answer: Assumption: the number of officials charged reflects how much corruption is taking place. It may be false because other factors could explain the reason given, or the link is not automatic. If it is false, the conclusion that corruption in Lunaria is falling is not supported.
items.markingKey: 1 mark assumption; 1 mark why it may be false (with example/alternative); 1 mark effect on conclusion [3]

items.stem: Read this argument: “Lunaria has more police officers per person than Merania. It follows that Lunaria is safer than Merania.” Identify the assumption, explain why it may be false, and explain the effect on the argument.
items.answer: Assumption: more police officers per person lead to lower crime. It may be false because other factors could explain the reason given, or the link is not automatic. If it is false, the conclusion that Lunaria is safer than Merania is not supported.
items.markingKey: 1 mark assumption; 1 mark why it may be false (with example/alternative); 1 mark effect on conclusion [3]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the argument that the voting age should be lowered to 16 depends on a questionable assumption? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: It assumes that 16-year-olds are mature enough to make informed voting decisions. If that assumption fails, the reasons do not lead to the conclusion. Against: Evidence such as “after Austria lowered the voting age to 16 in 2007, studies found that 16- and 17-year-olds turned out at rates similar to slightly older first-time voters” gives some support to the assumption. Most arguments on complex issues rely on reasonable assumptions. Judgement: A supported judgement tests the assumption against evidence and decides how far the argument survives.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by “assumption” in Global Perspectives?
options: Checking a possible assumption by asking whether the argument collapses if the statement is false.
Reasoning that is suggested but not stated directly in an argument.
An unstated reason that the argument depends on: if it is false, the conclusion does not follow.
items.answer: An unstated reason that the argument depends on: if it is false, the conclusion does not follow.
items.markingKey: Assumption: an unstated reason that the argument depends on: if it is false, the conclusion does not follow. [1]

items.stem: Read the argument about the use of economic sanctions. “Decades of US sanctions on Cuba since the 1960s have not changed its system of government. Targeted governments can blame foreigners for economic hardship. Moreover, ordinary citizens suffer more than the leaders responsible. So sanctions often strengthen rather than weaken the targeted regime. Some people claim that sanctions helped end apartheid in South Africa. However, in that case sanctions worked alongside strong internal resistance. Therefore, economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour.” Which of the following is an assumption the argument relies on?
options: Countries will keep to an agreement once it is signed
Sanctions often strengthen rather than weaken the targeted regime
The purpose of sanctions is to change the target’s behaviour rather than to signal disapproval
Targeted governments can blame foreigners for economic hardship
items.answer: The purpose of sanctions is to change the target’s behaviour rather than to signal disapproval
items.markingKey: Assumption: the purpose of sanctions is to change the target’s behaviour rather than to signal disapproval. The reason and IC are stated, so they are not assumptions; the fourth option is irrelevant. [1]

items.stem: Read the argument about disputes over shared rivers. “The Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan (1960) has survived several wars. Downstream countries depend on the river for drinking water and farming. Moreover, agreed rules reduce the risk of conflict. So shared rules can make water a source of cooperation rather than conflict. Some people claim that upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory. However, international water law also requires them not to cause significant harm to others. Therefore, upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours.” Explain how the counter-assertion challenges an assumption of the argument.
items.answer: The counter-assertion (upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory) suggests that the benefits claimed may come at a cost, questioning whether countries will keep to an agreement once it is signed is enough to justify the conclusion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark link counter to assumption; 1 mark effect on argument [2]

items.stem: Read this argument: “Merania holds elections every four years. It follows that Merania is a democracy.” Identify the assumption, explain why it may be false, and explain the effect on the argument.
items.answer: Assumption: regular elections are free and fair. It may be false because other factors could explain the reason given, or the link is not automatic. If it is false, the conclusion that Merania is a democracy is not supported.
items.markingKey: 1 mark assumption; 1 mark why it may be false (with example/alternative); 1 mark effect on conclusion; 1 mark suggests evidence that would test it [4]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a sequence in which one reason leads to an intermediate conclusion, which leads on to further conclusions”?
items.answer: Chain of reasoning
items.markingKey: Chain of reasoning: a sequence in which one reason leads to an intermediate conclusion, which leads on to further conclusions. [1]

items.stem: Arrange these statements into a chain of reasoning, ending with the main conclusion. P: Corruption thrives when deals are hidden from public view. Q: Every government should publish all public contracts online. R: Open contracting makes corruption harder to hide.
items.answer: P → R → Q
items.markingKey: Order: P → R → Q (reason(s) → intermediate conclusion → main conclusion). 2 marks fully correct; 1 mark if the conclusion is correctly last [2]

items.stem: Arrange these statements into a chain of reasoning, ending with the main conclusion. P: A single country can block action supported by most of the world. Q: The veto prevents the Council from fulfilling its responsibility for international peace. R: The permanent members were chosen in 1945 and do not reflect today’s world. S: The veto power of the permanent members should be restricted.
items.answer: P → R → Q → S
items.markingKey: Order: P → R → Q → S (reason(s) → intermediate conclusion → main conclusion). 2 marks fully correct; 1 mark if the conclusion is correctly last, 1 mark reasons before IC [3]

items.stem: Grace wrote this argument for a school debate: “After Ukraine introduced its ProZorro e-procurement system in 2016, many observers reported savings on public purchases. Corruption thrives when deals are hidden from public view. Moreover, publication allows journalists and citizens to act as watchdogs. So open contracting makes corruption harder to hide. Some people claim that publishing contracts could reveal commercially sensitive information. However, sensitive details can be redacted while prices and winners are published. Therefore, every government should publish all public contracts online.” Identify the counter-assertion and the response to it.
items.answer: Counter: publishing contracts could reveal commercially sensitive information. Response: sensitive details can be redacted while prices and winners are published.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Read the argument about the export of plastic waste to poorer countries. “Richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste. Much exported plastic is not recycled but burned or dumped. For example: After China’s 2018 import restrictions, Malaysia returned hundreds of containers of illegally imported plastic waste to their countries of origin. Furthermore, countries that consume the plastic should bear the cost of dealing with it. This shows that exporting waste shifts the harm onto poorer communities. It is sometimes argued that trade in sorted, clean plastic provides useful raw materials. But a ban could be limited to mixed and contaminated plastic.” (a) Describe the chain of reasoning that leads to the intermediate conclusion. (b) Write a counter-argument that a waste trading company might make.
items.answer: (a) Much exported plastic is not recycled but burned or dumped, and countries that consume the plastic should bear the cost of dealing with it; together these lead to the IC that exporting waste shifts the harm onto poorer communities. (b) A waste trading company argues the trade supplies raw materials, arguing that it earns profits from shipping waste, so the conclusion should be rejected or limited.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reasons; 1 mark link to IC [2] (b) 1 mark relevant counter-claim; 1 mark supporting reason [2]

items.stem: “The counter-argument that trade in sorted, clean plastic provides useful raw materials defeats the case that richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste.” Discuss this claim, considering arguments for and against before reaching a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: Trade in sorted, clean plastic provides useful raw materials. If the objection is strong, the reasons may not be enough. Against: A ban could be limited to mixed and contaminated plastic. The chain of reasoning (much exported plastic is not recycled but burned or dumped; exporting waste shifts the harm onto poorer communities) still stands. Judgement: A supported judgement decides whether the rebuttal answers the counter-argument and what evidence would settle it.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.answer: P → Q → R
items.markingKey: Order: P → Q → R (reason(s) → intermediate conclusion → main conclusion). 2 marks fully correct; 1 mark if the conclusion is correctly last [2]

items.answer: It shows the author has considered other perspectives; answering the strongest objection removes a reason to reject the conclusion and makes the argument more balanced and persuasive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark shows other perspectives considered; 1 mark response removes/weakens objection; 1 mark increases credibility/persuasiveness [3]

items.stem: “Countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Voluntary efforts have increased women’s representation only slowly. Rwanda’s constitution reserves 30% of seats for women, and women have held a majority of its lower house since 2008. Parliaments that reflect the population make better-informed laws. Against: Quotas mean candidates are chosen because of gender rather than ability. The argument assumes that having more women in parliament will change the decisions that parliament makes. Judgement: Judgement weighs the reasons and evidence against the counter-argument (response offered: quotas widen the pool of candidates and parties still choose among them).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Read the argument about migration caused by climate change. “(1) People displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status. (2) They are forced to leave their homes through no fault of their own. (3) For example: The UN Human Rights Committee ruled in the Teitiota case (2020) that states may not return people to places where climate change threatens their right to life. (4) Furthermore, the countries that caused most emissions have a duty to help those harmed. (5) This shows that climate migrants deserve the same protection as other forcibly displaced people. (6) It is sometimes argued that widening the definition could weaken protection for people fleeing persecution. (7) But a separate protocol could protect climate migrants without changing the 1951 Convention.” (a) Identify the main conclusion and the intermediate conclusion. (b) Describe the structure of the argument.
items.answer: (a) MC: people displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status. IC: climate migrants deserve the same protection as other forcibly displaced people. (b) Two reasons (with evidence) support the intermediate conclusion, which supports the main conclusion; a counter-assertion is raised and answered.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark reasons → IC; 1 mark IC → MC; 1 mark counter/response [3]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “reasoning that is suggested but not stated directly in an argument”?
items.answer: Implicit reasoning
items.markingKey: Implicit reasoning: reasoning that is suggested but not stated directly in an argument. [1]

items.stem: Ana argues: “Most newspapers in Korvia support the government. Therefore the government of Korvia is doing a good job.” Explain one unstated assumption that the argument makes.
items.answer: Assumption: newspaper support reflects the quality of government rather than ownership or pressure. If this is not true, the reason no longer supports the conclusion, so the argument fails.
items.markingKey: 1 mark assumption identified; 1 mark explains dependence (negation test) [2]

items.stem: “Ostrelia holds elections every four years, so Ostrelia is a democracy.” Identify one assumption in this argument and explain why the argument depends on it.
items.answer: Assumption: regular elections are free and fair. If this is not true, the reason no longer supports the conclusion, so the argument fails.
items.markingKey: 1 mark assumption identified; 1 mark explains dependence (negation test) [2]

items.stem: Read this argument: “Jovania introduced compulsory voting and turnout reached 92%. It follows that compulsory voting makes voters better informed.” Identify the assumption, explain why it may be false, and explain the effect on the argument.
items.answer: Assumption: people who are required to vote will learn more about politics. It may be false because other factors could explain the reason given, or the link is not automatic. If it is false, the conclusion that compulsory voting makes voters better informed is not supported.
items.markingKey: 1 mark assumption; 1 mark why it may be false (with example/alternative); 1 mark effect on conclusion [3]

items.stem: Read the argument about threats to press freedom. “Press freedom organisations have documented journalists jailed under “false news” laws in several countries. Such laws are vague and let officials decide what is true. Moreover, a free press is needed to expose corruption. So these laws are more often used to silence critics than to protect the public. Some people claim that false reports can cause panic during a crisis. However, existing laws on defamation and incitement already deal with genuinely harmful falsehoods. Therefore, governments should repeal broad “false news” laws.” (a) Identify one assumption in the argument. (b) Explain how the counter-assertion challenges an assumption of the argument.
items.answer: (a) Governments cannot be trusted to judge fairly what counts as false news. (b) The counter-assertion (false reports can cause panic during a crisis) suggests that the benefits claimed may come at a cost, questioning whether governments cannot be trusted to judge fairly what counts as false news is enough to justify the conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark link counter to assumption; 1 mark effect on argument [2]

items.stem: Tariq argues that the argument that social media companies should be legally responsible for false political content depends on a questionable assumption. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence.
items.answer: For: It assumes that companies are able to tell reliably which political claims are false. If that assumption fails, the reasons do not lead to the conclusion. Against: Evidence such as “the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal showed that data from millions of Facebook users had been harvested for political targeting” gives some support to the assumption. Most arguments on complex issues rely on reasonable assumptions. Judgement: A supported judgement tests the assumption against evidence and decides how far the argument survives.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by “chain of reasoning” in Global Perspectives?
options: Reasons that support a conclusion only when taken together.
An argument for a different or opposite conclusion.
Reasons that each support the conclusion on their own.
A sequence in which one reason leads to an intermediate conclusion, which leads on to further conclusions.
items.answer: A sequence in which one reason leads to an intermediate conclusion, which leads on to further conclusions.
items.markingKey: Chain of reasoning: a sequence in which one reason leads to an intermediate conclusion, which leads on to further conclusions. [1]

items.stem: Read: “Compulsory voting raises turnout. Separately, it makes parties campaign among all groups. Either reason alone supports introducing it in Ostrelia.” How do the reasons support the conclusion?
options: There are no reasons, only a conclusion
Each reason supports the conclusion on its own
The reasons support the conclusion only together
items.answer: Each reason supports the conclusion on its own
items.markingKey: Independent reasons. [1]

items.stem: Arrange these statements into a chain of reasoning, ending with the main conclusion. P: Shared rules can make water a source of cooperation rather than conflict. Q: Upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours. R: Agreed rules reduce the risk of conflict. S: Downstream countries depend on the river for drinking water and farming.
items.answer: S → R → P → Q
items.markingKey: Order: S → R → P → Q (reason(s) → intermediate conclusion → main conclusion). 2 marks fully correct; 1 mark if the conclusion is correctly last, 1 mark reasons before IC [3]

items.stem: Daniel wrote this argument for a school debate: “After Ukraine introduced its ProZorro e-procurement system in 2016, many observers reported savings on public purchases. Corruption thrives when deals are hidden from public view. Moreover, publication allows journalists and citizens to act as watchdogs. So open contracting makes corruption harder to hide. Some people claim that publishing contracts could reveal commercially sensitive information. However, sensitive details can be redacted while prices and winners are published. Therefore, every government should publish all public contracts online.” Write a counter-argument that a business association might make.
items.answer: A business association supports simpler procurement rules, arguing that complex rules raise costs for its members, so the conclusion should be rejected or limited.
items.markingKey: 1 mark relevant counter-claim; 1 mark supporting reason [2]

items.stem: Arjun wrote this argument for a school debate: “After Ukraine introduced its ProZorro e-procurement system in 2016, many observers reported savings on public purchases. Corruption thrives when deals are hidden from public view. Moreover, publication allows journalists and citizens to act as watchdogs. So open contracting makes corruption harder to hide. Some people claim that publishing contracts could reveal commercially sensitive information. However, sensitive details can be redacted while prices and winners are published. Therefore, every government should publish all public contracts online.” (a) Describe the chain of reasoning that leads to the intermediate conclusion. (b) Write a counter-argument that a business association might make.
items.answer: (a) Corruption thrives when deals are hidden from public view, and publication allows journalists and citizens to act as watchdogs; together these lead to the IC that open contracting makes corruption harder to hide. (b) A business association supports simpler procurement rules, arguing that complex rules raise costs for its members, so the conclusion should be rejected or limited.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reasons; 1 mark link to IC [2] (b) 1 mark relevant counter-claim; 1 mark supporting reason [2]

items.stem: Grace argues that the counter-argument that compulsory voting removes the freedom not to vote defeats the case that voting should be made compulsory. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence.
items.answer: For: Compulsory voting removes the freedom not to vote. If the objection is strong, the reasons may not be enough. Against: Voters may still spoil their ballot or choose “none of the above”. The chain of reasoning (a democracy works best when governments are chosen by the whole electorate; compulsory voting would make elected governments more representative) still stands. Judgement: A supported judgement decides whether the rebuttal answers the counter-argument and what evidence would settle it.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–3 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (4–6 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (7–9 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [9]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “facts, data, examples or expert testimony used to support a reason”?
items.answer: Evidence
items.markingKey: Evidence: facts, data, examples or expert testimony used to support a reason. [1]

items.stem: In an argument that every government should publish all public contracts online, the author writes: “Corruption thrives when deals are hidden from public view” and “After Ukraine introduced its ProZorro e-procurement system in 2016, many observers reported savings on public purchases”. Explain the difference between the role of these two statements.
items.answer: The first is a reason: a general claim that supports the conclusion. The second is evidence: a specific fact or example used to support a reason and make it more convincing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason identified and explained; 1 mark evidence identified and explained [2]

items.stem: Mateo wrote this argument for a school debate: “Decades of US sanctions on Cuba since the 1960s have not changed its system of government. Targeted governments can blame foreigners for economic hardship. Moreover, ordinary citizens suffer more than the leaders responsible. So sanctions often strengthen rather than weaken the targeted regime. Some people claim that sanctions helped end apartheid in South Africa. However, in that case sanctions worked alongside strong internal resistance. Therefore, economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour.” What is the function of “Moreover, ordinary citizens suffer more than the leaders responsible.” in this argument?
items.answer: Reason
items.markingKey: “Moreover, ordinary citizens suffer more than the leaders responsible.” is the reason. [1]

items.stem: Tomás wrote this argument for a school debate: “(1) After Ukraine introduced its ProZorro e-procurement system in 2016, many observers reported savings on public purchases. (2) Corruption thrives when deals are hidden from public view. (3) Moreover, publication allows journalists and citizens to act as watchdogs. (4) So open contracting makes corruption harder to hide. (5) Some people claim that publishing contracts could reveal commercially sensitive information. (6) However, sensitive details can be redacted while prices and winners are published. (7) Therefore, every government should publish all public contracts online.” (a) Identify the main conclusion. (b) Identify the evidence used.
items.answer: (a) Every government should publish all public contracts online (sentence 7). (b) After Ukraine introduced its ProZorro e-procurement system in 2016, many observers reported savings on public purchases (sentence 1).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Kwame wrote this argument for a school debate: “(1) The UN Human Rights Committee ruled in the Teitiota case (2020) that states may not return people to places where climate change threatens their right to life. (2) They are forced to leave their homes through no fault of their own. (3) Moreover, the countries that caused most emissions have a duty to help those harmed. (4) So climate migrants deserve the same protection as other forcibly displaced people. (5) Some people claim that widening the definition could weaken protection for people fleeing persecution. (6) However, a separate protocol could protect climate migrants without changing the 1951 Convention. (7) Therefore, people displaced by climate change should be given legal refugee status.” Identify the counter-assertion and explain how the author responds to it.
items.answer: Counter-assertion: widening the definition could weaken protection for people fleeing persecution. Response: a separate protocol could protect climate migrants without changing the 1951 Convention.
items.markingKey: 1 mark counter; 1 mark response [2]

items.stem: Read the argument about the export of plastic waste to poorer countries. “(1) After China’s 2018 import restrictions, Malaysia returned hundreds of containers of illegally imported plastic waste to their countries of origin. (2) Much exported plastic is not recycled but burned or dumped. (3) Moreover, countries that consume the plastic should bear the cost of dealing with it. (4) So exporting waste shifts the harm onto poorer communities. (5) Some people claim that trade in sorted, clean plastic provides useful raw materials. (6) However, a ban could be limited to mixed and contaminated plastic. (7) Therefore, richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste.” Identify two reasons given to support the intermediate conclusion.
items.answer: Much exported plastic is not recycled but burned or dumped; countries that consume the plastic should bear the cost of dealing with it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “Upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours.” Discuss this claim, considering arguments for and against before reaching a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: counter-arguments; assumptions.
items.answer: For: Downstream countries depend on the river for drinking water and farming. The Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan (1960) has survived several wars. Agreed rules reduce the risk of conflict. Against: Upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory. The argument assumes that countries will keep to an agreement once it is signed. Judgement: Judgement weighs the reasons and evidence against the counter-argument (response offered: international water law also requires them not to cause significant harm to others).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Read the argument about the spread of online disinformation during elections. “(1) The 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal showed that data from millions of Facebook users had been harvested for political targeting. (2) False political content can change how people vote. (3) Moreover, platforms profit from the engagement that false content attracts. (4) So platforms have both the power and the incentive to shape elections. (5) Some people claim that this would turn private companies into censors of political speech. (6) However, the law could be limited to clearly false factual claims, such as the wrong polling date. (7) Therefore, social media companies should be legally responsible for false political content.” (a) Describe the structure of the argument. (b) Suggest a further piece of evidence that would strengthen the argument.
items.answer: (a) Two reasons (with evidence) support the intermediate conclusion, which supports the main conclusion; a counter-assertion is raised and answered. (b) Comparative data from several countries, or a peer-reviewed study showing the effect claimed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reasons → IC; 1 mark IC → MC; 1 mark counter/response [3] (b) 1 mark relevant evidence; 1 mark why it strengthens [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “stated directly in the text”?
items.answer: Explicit
items.markingKey: Explicit: stated directly in the text. [1]

items.stem: Elena argues: “Zentara holds elections every four years. Therefore Zentara is a democracy.” Explain one unstated assumption that the argument makes.
items.answer: Assumption: regular elections are free and fair. If this is not true, the reason no longer supports the conclusion, so the argument fails.
items.markingKey: 1 mark assumption identified; 1 mark explains dependence (negation test) [2]

items.stem: “Pelora has more police officers per person than Valdoria, so Pelora is safer than Valdoria.” Identify one assumption in this argument and explain why the argument depends on it.
items.answer: Assumption: more police officers per person lead to lower crime. If this is not true, the reason no longer supports the conclusion, so the argument fails.
items.markingKey: 1 mark assumption identified; 1 mark explains dependence (negation test) [2]

items.stem: Sofia wrote this argument for a school debate: “Russia has vetoed draft resolutions on the war in Syria many times since 2011. A single country can block action supported by most of the world. Moreover, the permanent members were chosen in 1945 and do not reflect today’s world. So the veto prevents the Council from fulfilling its responsibility for international peace. Some people claim that the veto keeps the great powers inside the UN system. However, a restriction only in cases of mass atrocities would leave most of their influence intact. Therefore, the veto power of the permanent members should be restricted.” (a) Identify one assumption in the argument. (b) Explain how the counter-assertion challenges an assumption of the argument.
items.answer: (a) Without the veto the Council would act more effectively on crises. (b) The counter-assertion (the veto keeps the great powers inside the UN system) suggests that the benefits claimed may come at a cost, questioning whether without the veto the Council would act more effectively on crises is enough to justify the conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark link counter to assumption; 1 mark effect on argument [2]

items.stem: Read this argument: “A survey found 70% of people in Fendaria trust the army. It follows that the army should run the government of Fendaria.” Identify the assumption, explain why it may be false, and explain the effect on the argument.
items.answer: Assumption: an institution that is trusted should also govern. It may be false because other factors could explain the reason given, or the link is not automatic. If it is false, the conclusion that the army should run the government of Fendaria is not supported.
items.markingKey: 1 mark assumption; 1 mark why it may be false (with example/alternative); 1 mark effect on conclusion [3]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the argument that voting should be made compulsory depends on a questionable assumption.
items.answer: For: It assumes that governments chosen by more of the electorate will be more representative of the electorate’s interests. If that assumption fails, the reasons do not lead to the conclusion. Against: Evidence such as “In Australia, where voting is compulsory, turnout is usually above 90%” gives some support to the assumption. Most arguments on complex issues rely on reasonable assumptions. Judgement: A supported judgement tests the assumption against evidence and decides how far the argument survives.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by “counter-argument” in Global Perspectives?
options: A response that shows why a counter-argument is weak or does not defeat the main argument.
An argument for a different or opposite conclusion.
A sequence in which one reason leads to an intermediate conclusion, which leads on to further conclusions.
Reasons that each support the conclusion on their own.
items.answer: An argument for a different or opposite conclusion.
items.markingKey: Counter-argument: an argument for a different or opposite conclusion. [1]

items.stem: Read: “Party X won more seats than any other party in Nordavia. Party X has the support of a majority in parliament. So Party X can form a government alone.” How do the reasons support the conclusion?
options: Each reason supports the conclusion on its own
There are no reasons, only a conclusion
The reasons support the conclusion only together
items.answer: The reasons support the conclusion only together
items.markingKey: Joint reasons. [1]

items.stem: An argument concludes that upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours. Explain why including the counter-assertion “upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory” and the response “international water law also requires them not to cause significant harm to others” can make the argument stronger.
items.answer: It shows the author has considered other perspectives; answering the strongest objection removes a reason to reject the conclusion and makes the argument more balanced and persuasive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark shows other perspectives considered; 1 mark response removes/weakens objection; 1 mark increases credibility/persuasiveness [3]

items.stem: Grace wrote this argument for a school debate: “Decades of US sanctions on Cuba since the 1960s have not changed its system of government. Targeted governments can blame foreigners for economic hardship. Moreover, ordinary citizens suffer more than the leaders responsible. So sanctions often strengthen rather than weaken the targeted regime. Some people claim that sanctions helped end apartheid in South Africa. However, in that case sanctions worked alongside strong internal resistance. Therefore, economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour.” Write a counter-argument that a humanitarian NGO might make.
items.answer: A humanitarian NGO warns about harm to civilians, arguing that it delivers aid to the affected population, so the conclusion should be rejected or limited.
items.markingKey: 1 mark relevant counter-claim; 1 mark supporting reason [2]

items.stem: Kwame wrote this argument for a school debate: “Press freedom organisations have documented journalists jailed under “false news” laws in several countries. Such laws are vague and let officials decide what is true. Moreover, a free press is needed to expose corruption. So these laws are more often used to silence critics than to protect the public. Some people claim that false reports can cause panic during a crisis. However, existing laws on defamation and incitement already deal with genuinely harmful falsehoods. Therefore, governments should repeal broad “false news” laws.” (a) Describe the chain of reasoning that leads to the intermediate conclusion. (b) Write a counter-argument that Reporters Without Borders might make.
items.answer: (a) Such laws are vague and let officials decide what is true, and a free press is needed to expose corruption; together these lead to the IC that these laws are more often used to silence critics than to protect the public. (b) Reporters Without Borders condemns the restrictions, arguing that it is an NGO that defends press freedom, so the conclusion should be rejected or limited.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reasons; 1 mark link to IC [2] (b) 1 mark relevant counter-claim; 1 mark supporting reason [2]
